Review
Lipidomic analyses in epidemiology
Piyushkumar A. Mundra1, Jonathan E. Shaw1 and Peter J. Meikle1,2*
1Baker IDI Heart and Diabetes Institute, Melbourne, VIC, Australia and 2Department of Biochemistry
and Molecular Biology, University of Melbourne, Parkville, VIC, Australia
*Corresponding author. Baker IDI Heart and Diabetes Institute, 75 Commercial Rd, Melbourne, VIC 3004, Australia.
E-mail: peter.meikle@bakeridi.edu.au
Accepted 8 April 2016
Abstract
Clinical lipid measurements have been the mainstay of risk assessment for chronic dis-
ease since the Framingham study commenced over 60 years ago. Thousands of subse-
quent epidemiological studies have provided much insight into the relationship between
plasma lipid proﬁles, health and disease. However, the human lipidome consists of thou-
sands of individual lipid species, and current lipidomic technology presents us with an
unprecedented opportunity to measure lipid phenotypes, representing genomic, meta-
bolic, diet and lifestyle-related exposures, in large epidemiological studies. The number
of epidemiological studies using lipidomic proﬁling is increasing and has the potential to
provide improved biological and clinical insight into human disease. In this review, we
discuss current lipidomic technologies, epidemiological studies using these technologies
and the statistical approaches used in the analysis of the resulting data. We highlight the
potential of integrating genomic and lipidomic datasets and discuss the future opportuni-
ties and challenges in this emerging ﬁeld.
Introduction
Lipidomics refers to the characterization, analysis and
study of the lipid complement of biological systems. The
biological system in question may be at the cellular, tissue
or organism level. However, in large-scale human studies,
the lipidome under investigation is typically a biological
fluid (the plasma lipidome) as this is the biological material
most readily available from research participants. Other
lipidomes examined in this context include urine,1 tear,2
saliva3 and erythrocyte4 lipidomes. In this review we will,
for the most part, focus on the plasma lipidome.
From an epidemiological perspective, there have been a
vast number of studies examining the traditional clinical
lipid measures of plasma [total cholesterol, triglycerides,
high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) and low-
density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)].5–7 Each of these
measures represents the sum of a complex mixture of mo-
lecular species of free cholesterol and cholesteryl ester or
triacylglycerol present in the lipoprotein particles. These
measures capture the bulk components of the plasma lipi-
dome and provide some insight into the relative distribu-
tion between lipoprotein pools, but they do not capture the
full complexity of the plasma lipidome.
The bulk of plasma lipids exist within the different lipo-
protein pools [very low-density lipoprotein (VLDL), LDL
and HDL]; each of these represents a pool of complex par-
ticles made up of differing proportions of protein and lipid.
The common structural characteristic of these particles is

the polar lipid surface of the particle, which consists pri-
marily of phospholipid, sphingolipid and free cholesterol,
which surrounds the hydrophobic core, primarily choles-
teryl ester and triacylglycerol. Within each of these lipid
classes there are tens to hundreds of individual molecular
species that collectively make up the plasma lipidome.
Other components of the plasma lipidome include lyso-
phospholipids, fatty acids and their metabolites. These
components are partitioned between the lipoprotein pools
and the albumin fraction of plasma. In total there are
many hundreds or thousands of lipids that are accessible to
lipidomic analysis using current technology.8,9 The appli-
cation of lipidomic technology to the plasma lipidome and
to individual lipoprotein lipidomes has improved our
understanding of the complex structure-function relation-
ships that exist within these particles and highlighted the
importance of lipids in all aspects of lipoprotein metabol-
ism and dysfunction.4,10–12
A primary role of plasma lipoproteins is the transport
of lipids between the gut, liver and peripheral tissue beds;
the plasma lipidome can therefore reflect underlying meta-
bolic processes that may be influenced by dietary, environ-
mental and genetic factors. Whereas many anthropometric
and clinical measures [body mass index (BMI), HDL, sys-
tolic blood pressure (SBP)] also reflect the combination of
environmental and genetic influences, lipidomic studies
have the potential to provide a uniquely detailed readout
of these complex metabolic pathways and interactions.
There have been many lipidomic analyses of relatively
small case-control studies, examining the relationship be-
tween plasma lipids and disease states.4,13–17 Many of
these studies use bioinformatic approaches in the analysis
of lipidomic data to inform on the relationships between
lipid measures and clinical outcomes and for the discovery
of potential biomarkers for these disease states. However,
a limitation of such studies is that they do not capture the
inherent heterogeneity of human populations and so are
unable to dissect out the relative contribution of lipids
from the many potential confounders to disease aetiology.
As lipidomic studies increase in size (of the cohort
studied) and complexity (of the lipidome analysed), the po-
tential to consider the lipidome in an epidemiological con-
text arises. This provides the opportunity to obtain a more
complete understanding of disease aetiology including the
influences and interactions of anthropometric, clinical and
lifestyle factors on the lipidome and on disease outcomes.
However, whereas population size in epidemiological stud-
ies is a strength, along with the large number of lipids
measured, it brings the technical challenges associated with
measuring several hundred lipid species across several
thousand samples while maintaining sufficient quality con-
trol to produce a useful dataset. Such datasets then require
integration of epidemiological analytical strategies into lip-
idomic analyses to fully realise the potential of these
studies.
Ultimately
lipidomics,
as
with
all
‘omics’,
is
a
hypothesis-generating exercise. Such hypotheses may relate
to how we understand disease pathogenesis, identification
of new biomarkers for disease or potentially new thera-
peutic targets. Understanding the lipidome at a population
level will increase our confidence in these hypotheses and
facilitate the design of future validation studies. Here we
present the current state of lipidomic analyses in epidemi-
ology and discuss future challenges and opportunities.
Lipidomic Technologies
There are many different approaches to lipidomic analyses
and the reader is referred to recent reviews in this area.18,19
Here we discuss briefly the technologies as they relate to
epidemiological studies and the specific requirements of
such studies.
In order to obtain maximum detail at a molecular (lipid
species) level, mass spectrometry-based lipidomic strategies
have emerged as the most powerful. Here also there are
multiple approaches using high mass resolution instru-
ments [Time of Flight (TOF) or Orbitrap] or lower reso-
lution
instruments
such
as
triple
quadrapole
mass
spectrometers, each of which is typically coupled with a
soft
ionization
(electrospray)
source.
The
two
main
approaches involve either direct infusion analysis (shotgun
lipidomics), now typically performed on high resolution
instruments,18
or
liquid
chromatography
mass
spectrometry-based lipidomics.9,19 Other approaches such
as gas chromatography or capillary electrophoresis have
been coupled with mass spectrometry for lipidomic stud-
ies,20 but these provide a more restricted coverage of the
lipidome and so are typically used for studies focused on
specific lipid classes.
Direct infusion or shotgun lipidomic approaches offer
several advantages; the continuous infusion of the sample
enables multiple consecutive experiments to be performed
for the identification and quantification of lipid species, in
consistent ion suppression for all lipid measurements, po-
tentially leading to improved accuracy. However, direct in-
fusion is more susceptible to the influence of extraneous
salts, and so lipid extraction is typically more demanding
and must deal with the differential partitioning of the more
polar lipids in the two-phase solvent extraction systems. In
contrast, liquid chromatography mass spectrometry-based
lipidomics offers the advantage of an additional dimension
of separation of the lipids. This enables the use of single-
phase lipid extraction methods, as the contaminating salts
can be removed during the chromatographic step, and

reduces many of the complexities resulting from isomeric
(same composition but different structure), isotopic (same
composition and structure but different mass) and isobaric
(same nominal mass but different composition) lipid spe-
cies which can often, but not always, be separated chroma-
tographically. However, these advantages come at a cost
of analysis time associated with the chromatography and
the need to perform the mass spectrometric experiments
within the chromatographic timescale. Ultimately, lipido-
mic approaches are a compromise between analysis time,
coverage of the lipidome and the accuracy and precision of
the analysis. For epidemiological studies with hundreds to
thousands of samples, analysis time, instrument stability
and precision (repeatability) of the analytics are primary
considerations to minimize technical variance and provide
maximum power in subsequent statistical analyses.
Raw data acquired from lipidomic experiments in the
form of signal intensities or chromatogram areas are typic-
ally normalized to the corresponding signals from one or
more internal standards to provide quantitative measures
of individual lipids. Internal standards are ideally stable
isotope analogues of the lipid of interest but often are
structurally related, non-physiological lipid species.9 For
any
large
scale
lipidomic
experiment,
limitations
to
throughput often require larger sample sets to be split into
smaller batches for sample preparation, extraction and lip-
idomic analysis. Analysing such batches over a large period
of time (days, weeks or months) can increase technical
variation which must be appropriately dealt with before
any further data analysis.21,22
It should also be noted that the distribution of relative
concentrations of lipid species is generally right-skewed
and non-Gaussian and so requires transformation (for ex-
ample, log transformation) to approach a normal distribu-
tion;
alternatively,
non-parametric
tests
should
be
applied.23 Finally, as the concentration of circulating lipid
species varies by several orders of magnitude, the concen-
tration of each lipid species is often expressed as a multiple
of its interquartile range or standard deviation to facilitate
ease of interpretation in subsequent association studies.
After preprocessing the data, the resultant lipidomic
measurements form a block data structure, where lipid spe-
cies within a given class/subclass are often, but not always,
highly inter-correlated. This is predominantly attributed to
the common metabolic pathways of lipid species within
classes and subclasses. The inclusion of a large number of
redundant features poses a challenge for subsequent multi-
variate statistical analysis and several approaches have
been proposed to deal with this. One can use a single repre-
sentative lipid species from each class/subclass, or sum the
species within a class for further analysis, but such
approaches do not capture the full complexity of the
available data. An unsupervised clustering approach (for
example, k-means or hierarchical clustering) can be per-
formed for data reduction, but this typically results in class
specific clusters. Alternately, it is possible to reduce the
data using additional -omics or epidemiological measure-
ments collected for a given cohort. In a lipidomic analysis
of the San Antonio Family Heart Study (SAFHS), genetic
correlations resulting from pedigree information were used
to reduce 319 lipid species to 12 genetic clusters, and sub-
sequent analysis identified associations between some clus-
ters and risk factors of cardiovascular disease (CVD)
including central obesity, type 2 diabetes (T2D), raised
serum triglycerides and metabolic syndrome.24
In the absence of such measurements the dataset may be
reduced
using
data-driven
dimensionality
reduction
approaches such as principal components or partial least
square scores.25,26 However, these results are often diffi-
cult to interpret, because the groups of lipid species may
not have any clear biological meaning. Recently, an un-
supervised feature reduction approach, LICRE, was de-
veloped to reduce the feature redundancy in lipidomics
data by using the maximum spanning tree, soft mean shift
clustering and relevance network.27 LICRE provides a
non-redundant set of lipid species which help in the devel-
opment of predictive models but may remove lipids in-
formative
to
the
underlying
biology.
Ultimately,
an
unsupervised data reduction, either by LICRE or by any
clustering approach, is useful for risk prediction modelling
but at the expense of limiting biological interpretation. To
understand underlying biology through association studies,
it is important to analyse complete data.
At the same time, with hundreds of lipidomic measure-
ments, correction for multiple comparisons is essential for
any meaningful statistical inference. Two approaches have
typically been employed: controlling false discovery rate
(FDR, for example, the Benjamini-Hochberg method) or
controlling
the
family-wise
error
rate
(FWER,
the
Bonferroni method). The FWER approach controls the
probability of making a type I error (false positives)
whereas the FDR approach controls for the expected pro-
portions of false positives. Given that lipidomic measure-
ments are typically collinear in nature and that cohorts are
relatively small (i.e. with limited statistical power), the
Benjamini-Hochberg method28 is often used rather than
the more stringent control for FWER obtained with the
Bonferroni method.
Association Studies
One of the principal objectives of epidemiological lipido-
mics is to identify how lipid species are related to biolo-
gical or clinical outcomes. In cross-sectional studies,

Cross sectional analysis
Many plasma lipids show strong associations with mul-
tiple anthropometric, clinical and lifestyle characteristics,
including age, gender, BMI, blood pressure and diet,
among others. The identification of such lipids is an im-
portant step towards understanding the complex signalling
and metabolic pathways involved in disease processes. In a
large cohort from the KORA F4 study (1038 females and
1124 males with age range of 32–81 years), 71 metabolites
were associated with age including species of acylcarnitine,
sphingomyelin,
phosphatidylcholine,
alkylphosphatidyl-
choline and lysophosphatidylcholine.29 In the SAFHS
(1012 participants), 148 of 312 lipid species were associ-
ated with age after adjustment for sex, BMI, SBP, 2-h
post-load glucose and smoking status.9 Although the
cross-validation between these two studies is limited by the
lipids analysed in each, good agreement was observed for
sphingomyelin as well as ether- and lysophospholipids.
In the same analysis, 200 of the 312 lipid species were
associated with BMI after adjusting for sex, age, SBP, 2-h
post load glucose and smoking status, and 223 lipid species
were associated with sex (adjusted for age, BMI, SBP, 2-h
post load glucose and smoking status). This study vali-
dated and added to several smaller studies that had re-
ported on subsets of these lipids in different clinical
settings.30–33
To decipher the association of plasma lipidomic profiles
with hypertension in the SAFHS cohort, polygenic regres-
sion models, liability threshold models and bivariate trait
analyses adjusting for age, age2, sex, age x sex interaction,
age2 x sex interaction, HDL and LDL fractions, BMI, insu-
lin resistance index (HOMA-IR0, lipid-lowering medica-
tion use and antihypertensive drug use were applied.34 The
results showed that diacylglycerols in general, and the
diacylglycerol species DG16:0/22:5 and DG16:0/22:6 in
particular, were strongly associated with systolic blood
pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure and mean arterial
pressure.
These larger studies demonstrate the strong association
of lipids with many anthropometric and clinical measure-
ments and highlight the need to adjust for these covariates
if we are to accurately define associations with disease.
Further, depending on the study objective, it may also be

measurements (cholesterol, HDL-C and triglycerides) and
medications, particularly lipid-lowering drugs.
Lipidomic profiling has been used to characterize dis-
ease states relative to healthy controls, and to better under-
stand disease progression. It is well established that
dyslipidaemia is associated with T2D. However, the rela-
tionship between lipid metabolism and progression from
normal glucose tolerance to impaired glucose tolerance
(prediabetes) and subsequently to T2D was less clear.
Using a subcohort from the Australian Diabetes, Obesity
and Lifestyle Study (AusDiab) and an independent valid-
ation cohort from the SAFHS, logistic regression adjusted
for age, sex, waist circumference and SBP was used to iden-
tify lipids associated with prediabetes and T2D compared
with normal glucose-tolerant subjects. This demonstrated
that the alterations in lipid metabolism, involving over 100
lipid species across nine classes and subclasses, associated
with T2D were also present in the prediabetic state before
the onset of T2D, implying that the change in lipid metab-
olism leading to these altered plasma lipid profiles precede
the onset of frank diabetes.35 Eight out of nine classes/sub-
classes (except alkylphosphatidylcholine) were associated
similarly in an independent SAFHS cohort. In other
independent but smaller studies, ceramides, phospholipids
and triacylglycerol have been found to be positively associ-
ated with type 2 diabetes, further strengthening the import-
ance of these lipid classes in T2D.17,31,33,36
In a similar study, plasma lipidomic profiling was used
to examine the relationship between stable and unstable
coronary artery disease (CAD).37 On a small cohort of 220
individuals (stable CAD n ¼ 60; unstable CAD n ¼ 80;
matched healthy controls n ¼ 80), logistic regression ad-
justed for age, sex, BMI, SBP, fasting blood glucose and
statin use was performed. Thirteen lipid classes and 102 in-
dividual lipid species were found to be associated with sta-
ble CAD (compared with healthy controls), and five lipid
classes and 50 lipid species were found associated with un-
stable CAD (compared with stable CAD). These types of
studies are starting to provide some insight into the rela-
tionship
between
lipid
metabolism
and
disease
progression.
In family-based cohorts such as SAFHS and the Leiden
Longevity Study, a Dutch family-based study, pedigree in-
formation is available. In genetic studies, large pedigrees
are useful as they provide multiple copies of rare variants
and thus increase the statistical power to find genetic

circulating metabolites including lipids, and hence associ-
ation studies should also consider genetic relatedness. The
simplest approach is to include a term in the regression
model which considers data from the same family as a
group.38 However, techniques such as polygenic regres-
sion, taking pedigree structure into account, performed
with the SOLAR (Sequential Oligogenic Linkage Analysis
Routines) software, allow for the estimation of the effects
of other variables independent of the familial component,
thereby removing the possible confounding of shared gen-

and

power
of
the

In 742 people from a Dutch family-based study, the re-
lationship between plasma phospho- and sphingolipid spe-
cies and depression/anxiety symptoms were measured
using a linear mixed model of variance component meth-
odology with polygenic regression taking pedigree infor-
mation into account.40 Sphingomyelin [SM(23:1)] and
alkylphosphatidylcholine [PC(O-36:4)] species were found
to be negatively associated with several depression/anxiety
measurements. In an independent cohort from the same
population, PC(O-36:4) was again found to be associated
with depression scores. For further details on such models,
readers are referred to Blangero et al.41
Longitudinal analysis
Though cross-sectional case-control cohort studies have
been extensively used for lipidomic analyses, they are not
able to identify prognostic markers, nor infer causality be-
tween lipids and clinical outcomes. Longitudinal studies
relating lipids measured at baseline with outcomes deter-
mined over time can start to address these issues.
Choosing an appropriate analysis method and checking
the statistical assumptions of the method are important.
Depending on the cohort design, logistic regression, Cox
regression or weighted Cox regression have been applied in
longitudinal lipidomics studies. In situations where exact
time to event is not available, logistic regression comparing
baseline lipid measures with outcomes at a defined time
point have been used. To identify lipids associated with in-
cident CVD [defined as myocardial infarction (MI), ischae-
mic stroke (stroke) or CVD-related death], top-down
shotgun lipidomics was applied on a subcohort of the pro-
spective population-based Malmo¨ Diet and Cancer (MDC)
study (211 CVD cases and 216 controls).42 The associ-
ations were determined using logistic regression adjusting
for Framingham risk factors (age, sex, diabetes, smoking
status, LDL-cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, SBP, BMI and
use of antihypertensive treatment). Species of lysophospha-
tidylcholine, sphingomyelin and triacylglycerol were found
to be associated with incident CVD. The Framingham risk
score is widely used in clinical practice to estimate the risk
of coronary events. Identification of lipids associated
with CVD independent of Framingham risk factors demon-
strates that lipids may provide additional information in
risk assessment. It is worth noting that the amalgamation
of clinical outcomes (i.e. myocardial infarct, stroke and
CVD death) into a single outcome can provide greater
power in the analysis, but differences in aetiologies and as-
sociations with specific events may be missed. However,
such outcome stratification will typically require larger
studies.
Where time to event data are available, the opportunity
to use Cox regression is presented. Here the proportional
hazards assumption must be tested by first computing the
significance level from the Schoenfeld residual tests for all
variables. If these assumptions hold for each variable, then
Cox regression is appropriate. However, for case cohort
studies weighted Cox regression is required; this applies
differential weights to the un-enriched samples and the
additional cases. An example of this approach is provided
in a recent analysis of incident T2D in a nested case-cohort
substudy of the EPIC study (12403 T2D cases across eight
European countries).20 Weighted Cox regression adjusted
for age, collection centre, sex, physical activity, smoking
status, education level, total energy intake, alcohol intake
and BMI indicated that odd-chain (C15:0 and C17:0) and
long-chain (C20:0, C22:0, C23:0 and C24:0) saturated
fatty acids were negatively associated with incident T2D.
Conversely, short-chain saturated fatty acids (C14:0,
C16:0 and C18:0) were positively associated with incident
T2D. Correlation with self-reported dietary intake sug-
gested that odd-chain fatty acids were associated with
dairy products, whereas even-chain saturated fatty acids
were highly correlated with alcohol, soft drinks and pota-
toes. Importantly, this study highlights how lipids can be
used to link lifestyle factors with clinical endpoints and
thereby provide evidence for causal pathways and the po-
tential role of lipids in disease pathogenesis.
In population-based studies (without enrichment of out-
comes) Cox regression may be appropriate. To identify the
circulating metabolites, including lipid species, associated
with incident CVD (defined as hospitalization or death
with a primary diagnosis for acute myocardial infarction
or unstable angina), an untargeted metabolomic study was
performed on 1028 individuals (131 events; 10-year me-
dian follow-up) with validation in 1670 individuals (282
events; 3.9-year median follow-up).43 The cohorts were
obtained from the TwinGene, Uppsala Longitudinal Study
of Adult Men (ULSAM) and the Prospective Investigation
of the Vasculature in Uppsala Seniors (PIVUS). In the
ULSAM cohort, 32 metabolites were associated with CVD

In a similar study, Stegmann et al. investigated the asso-
ciation of plasma lipids with future cardiovascular events
in 685 samples (followed for 10 years; 90 events) from the
prospective population-based Bruneck Study using shotgun
targeted lipidomics.44 Species of cholesteryl ester, lyso-
phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidyle-
thanolamine,
sphingomyelin
and
triacylglycerol
were
associated with future events (adjusted for age, gender and
statin treatment) and the fatty acids comprising these lipids
were subsequently validated in a subcohort of the UK
Twin Registry data (n ¼ 1453, 45 cases).
These cross-sectional and longitudinal studies are now
starting to demonstrate concordance in the associations of
specific lipid classes/subclasses with different disease states.
In all, three longitudinal studies and one cross-sectional
study have each shown sphingomyelin, lysophosphatidyl-
choline and triacylglycerol to be associated with cardiovas-
cular disease. As shown in Figure 1, these represent three
distinct but interconnected pathways, suggesting that mul-
tiple mechanisms interact in a complex manner in cardio-
vascular disease pathogenesis. These studies are important
as they also provide translational links between animal
studies and human health. In type 2 diabetes, we and
others have demonstrated the associations of ceramide
metabolic pathways providing a direct link with the many
animal studies examining this relationship.45 These associ-
ations can also be tracked to earlier stages of the disease
(prediabetes and obesity), to delineate temporal and poten-
tially causal pathways in disease pathogenesis. Although
we are starting to see concordance between studies at a
lipid class/subclass level, such replications are not observed
for the majority of individual lipid species due to difference
in instruments, coverage, analytical approaches and poten-
tially cohort characteristics. Further developments in the
instrumentation and alignment of methodologies will lead
to better concordance at lipid species level in the future.
Despite such limitations, these studies are providing a
growing body of evidence to demonstrate that circulating
lipid species are associated with metabolic outcomes, inde-
pendent of traditional risk factors, and may therefore be
useful in the identification of high-risk individuals for tar-
geted treatment strategies.
Risk Prediction Modelling
Lipidomic data require special consideration in terms of
multivariate model development. From the hundreds of
lipid variables, many of which are highly correlated, the
challenge is to identify informative, independent bio-
markers to create a multivariate model with a minimum
number of biomarkers and optimal performance. Ideally
this should be performed within a cross-validation frame-
work, to avoid over-fitting of the data. Whereas transla-
tion of such models into clinical tests and screening assays
is a clear priority, the modelling process itself can identify
lipids that may also represent viable therapeutic targets.
As discussed earlier, one approach is to reduce the data
dimensionality using techniques such as partial least
squares or principal components. However, biological in-
terpretation and clinical translation of such models is chal-
lenging. Thus, a feature selection approach may be more
appropriate. Penalized regression techniques, such as Lasso
and Elastic net, provide an opportunity for automatic
feature selection within the model building process.46,47
In
lipidomics,
this
approach
has
started
to
gain
attention.14,15,44
Stegmann et al. used Lasso within a 10-fold cross-
validation framework (repeated 1000 times) to identify fu-
ture cardiovascular events. Six lipid species (cholesteryl
ester CE(16:1), triacylglycerol TG(54:2), phosphatidyle-
thanolamine PE(36:5), sphingomyelin SM(34:2) and the
lysophosphatidylcholine species LPC(20:5), and LPC(22:6)
were identified.44 A prediction model containing these six
lipid species and traditional risk factors (age, sex, history
of diabetes mellitus, smoking status, systolic blood pres-
sure, total cholesterol and HDL cholesterol) resulted in a
3.76% improvement in the C-statistic and a 14.9% im-
provement in the categorical net reclassification index
(NRI) (for 10-year risk) compared with the risk factors
only model.
Similarly, Mapstone et al. performed one of the first
longitudinal studies on Alzheimer’s disease and identified
10 lipidomic-based biomarkers using a receiver operating
curve (ROC) regularized learning technique based on
Lasso penalty (within a 10-fold cross-validation) to distin-
guish between amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI)
or mild Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and, importantly, con-
verters from non-impaired memory status, and healthy

The identified lipid species in these studies were partially

selection techniques used in classification and regres-
sion48,49 may also be useful for development of lipidomic-
based risk predictive algorithms. However, these will re-

Epidemiological analyses using high-dimensional lipido-
mic data should be performed in a machine learning frame-
work, particularly for the development of clinical decision
support systems.50 Approaches such as cross-validation
and bootstrapping should be employed to control for ove-
fitting and optimistic performance estimates. In addition, a
thorough evaluation of model performance including esti-
mates of sensitivity, specificity and net reclassification
index should be performed. A number of reviews discuss-
ing these issues in lipidomics are available.23,25,51–53
Integration of Lipidomic and Genomic Data
Lipid metabolism and circulating plasma lipids are influ-
enced
by
both
genetic
and
environmental
factors.
Combined lipidomic/genomic studies not only allows us to
define the relative contribution of genetics and environ-
ment to the variation in plasma lipids, but also has the po-
tential to provide evidence for causality via Mendelian
randomization. Importantly, lipids represent endopheno-
types with a clear genetic component that can potentially
be used to bridge the complex biology linking genetic vari-
ance with disease outcomes.
There have been many genome-wide association studies
(GWAS) on clinical lipid measurements. Recently, identifi-
cation of new loci and refinement of known loci influencing
LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides and total
cholesterol have been reported. Willer et al. examined
188 577 individuals using genome-wide and custom geno-
typing arrays and identified 157 loci, out of which 62 were
new associations with lipid levels in humans.54 The loci
associated with blood lipid levels were often associated with
disease traits (including CVD and T2D) and other physio-
logical factors (blood pressure, waist-hip ratio and BMI).
In contrast, there are relatively very few studies relating
sequence variation to lipidomic data. Sphingolipids play
important structural and signalling roles in disease patho-
genesis. To study the influence of genetic variants on
circulating levels of 33 sphingolipids and 43 matched me-
tabolite ratios, a genome-wide association study was per-
formed on 4400 subjects from five diverse European
populations. The GenABEL package in R was used to iden-
tify the association between the age- and sex-adjusted
residuals of sphingolipid traits (both as absolute concentra-
tions and as relative content of the total sphingolipid pool:
mol%) and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) geno-
types.55 Four of the five loci identified contained genes
encoding proteins which were directly responsible for de
novo ceramide synthesis or for ceramide re-synthesis from
sphingosine/sphinganine-phosphates or both. The associ-
ations were also observed with sphingomyelins, suggesting
a conversion of a large proportion of ceramide into more
stable ‘sphingomyelin-pool’.
More recently, Laurila et al. performed integrated ana-
lysis of transcriptomic, genomic and lipidomic data on a
Finnish population to inform on the genetics of HDL-C.56
Logistic regression was used to identify associations be-
tween high/low HDL-C status and transcriptomic or SNP
data (adjusted for age, sex and BMI). The HDL particle
lipidome data were then analysed by comparing the con-
centration of each lipid in the HDL particles between the
low- and high-HDL groups. The effect of genetic risk
scores (based on the SNP analysis) on gene expression, lipi-
domic profiling and biochemical markers of inflammation
was determined using a linear regression approach. The re-
sults demonstrated that genetic variants within inflamma-
tory pathways were enriched among subjects with low
HDL-C status, and the lipidomic data showed an associ-
ation between the antioxidant lipidomic pathway and the
genetic risk score. Plasmalogens and lysophosphatidylcho-
lines were enriched in the HDL particles derived from sub-
jects with high HDL-C, whereas ceramide (d18:1/20:1)
and different types of triacylglycerol were enriched in the
HDL particles derived from subjects with low HDL-C.
While these analytical strategies are still in their infancy,
the development in whole-genome sequencing and advanced
lipidomic technologies provides the framework for further,
more detailed studies that will help to define not only the
mechanisms controlling lipid homeostasis but also how
these can contribute to disease pathogenesis and risk.
Conclusions
Current literature on large-scale lipidomic studies demon-
strates that individual lipid classes, subclasses and species
are altered in specific disease states and, as discussed
above, concordance of these studies is good and is improv-
ing as the extent of the lipid profiles and size of the cohorts
increase. Two general observations can now be made in re-
lation to lipid metabolism, homeostasis and disease patho-
genesis. First, sphingolipids and, in particular, ceramide
and sphingomyelin are key mediators of inflammatory dis-
ease and this is now seen at a population level. This evi-
dence provides support for the targeting of these metabolic
pathways in new therapeutic strategies to alleviate the

Future Opportunities and Challanges
Over the past decade, lipidomics has made an increasing
contribution to our understanding of lipid metabolism and
homeostasis. As technology has improved, so our ability to
obtain more complex lipidomic profiles from larger sample
sets has increased. These developments now provide us
with
the
opportunity
to
integrate
lipidomics
into
epidemiology.
The power of epidemiological lipidomics lies in the abil-
ity to identify associations of individual lipid species and/or
lipid metabolic pathways with anthropometric and clinical
outcomes, independent of the many confounding factors
that may also contribute to lipid homeostasis. Whereas
many early studies were cross-sectional and lacked inde-
pendent validation, more recent longitudinal studies have
demonstrated the potential of lipidomics to predict clinical
outcomes in a number of disease states independently of
traditional risk factors and, importantly, are validating these
associations both within and between studies.
To maximize outcomes from these studies will require on-
going development of statistical and bioinformatic approaches
to deal with the complex and often collinear data. In particu-
lar, new approaches to data integration, feature selection and
model development will be required to maximize the outcomes
from these studies. With these developments, epidemiological
lipidomics has the potential to improve our understanding of
the role of lipids in health and disease, identify new therapeutic
targets and develop improved risk assessment and diagnostic
markers for many disease states.
